comments.author: tokenring
comments.text: Given my handle I feel personally addressed by chapter 4. For the record: deterministic latency was a real advantage, and some of us maintained rings well into an era when it was deeply unfashionable. The protocols didn't fail, the economics did.

replies.author: gopherhole
replies.text: OP here — that's basically the thesis of the whole guide. Almost none of these protocols were abandoned for technical reasons. They lost procurement battles, or their one committed vendor pivoted, or they solved a problem that stopped existing. Writing the obituaries fairly meant separating the engineering from the funeral.

replies.author: pagetable
replies.text: The exception being the ones that died of their own extensibility. A few of those protocols collapsed under optional-feature matrices no two implementations agreed on. That's a technical death, just a slow one.

comments.author: lambdacurious
comments.text: Is there a companion list of abandoned protocols that quietly refuse to die? I keep finding twenty-year-old field equipment chattering away in serial dialects that officially ceased to exist. Abandonment is a spectrum, and the far end of it is "still running in a pump station nobody can find the keys to."

comments.author: octetstream
comments.text: Minor nit: the guide describes the handshake in section 9 as three-way, but the original spec allowed a two-way fast path when the responder had cached state. I only know this because I implemented it wrong once, in both directions.
